results.title: AWS just raised reserved GPU prices again. This is the fourth hike this year. | Spheron Network
highlights:
AWS just raised reserved GPU prices again. This is the fourth hike this year.

Effective Oct 7, AWS Capacity Block rates climb to $5.97/hr for H100 (up from $5.19) and $16.15/hr for B300. That puts H100 and B300 on AWS up 40 to 75% since January.

Our marketplace rate for H100 is still $2.01/hr. For B300 it is $5.85/hr. Neither has moved all year.

Our H100 rate is 66% below AWS's new rate, and our B300 rate is 64% below AWS's new rate, for the same chip on the same day. Spheron is a marketplace, not a single cloud, so prices do not quietly creep up every quarter.

Compare it against whatever you are paying today for the same GPU.

results.title: RunPod Secure Cloud GPU Rates Rise: H100 $3.99, B200 $7.99
highlights:
A GPU price tracker, GPU Economy, says RunPod raised 12 of its 29 on-demand Secure Cloud GPU rates on 8 October 2026 [1]. RunPod’s pricing page now shows the higher prices [2]. RunPod made no announcement that we could find, so the timing and the old prices rest on the tracker.

## The new rates

RunPod sells two tiers, Secure Cloud and Community Cloud; on its listings the Community rates are lower. Prices are in US dollars per GPU per hour, on demand, meaning pay as you go. GPU Economy reports [1]:

| GPU | Before | Now | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM | $3.49 | $3.99 | +14.3% |
| H200 | $4.59 | $5.29 | +15.3% |
| B200 | $6.79 | $7.99 | +17.7% |
| B300 | $7.89 | $8.99 | +13.9% |

The H100, H200, B200 and B300 are Nvidia data-centre chips used to train and run AI models. The tracker says the 12 rises came “between our reads of October 8, 2026 at 15:41 and 16:41 UTC”, which is 16:41 and 17:41 in London. It also computes that one H100 SXM running for a 730-hour month went from $2,547.70 to $2,912.70.

## What did not change

The tracker says “None of the 35 Community Cloud on-demand rates changed in the same read”: the H100 SXM there stayed at $2.69 and the B200 at $5.98 [1].

...

RunPod’s pricing page lists $3.99/hr for the H100 SXM, $7.99/hr for the B200, $5.29/hr for the H200 and $8.99/hr for the B300 [2]. But the page is labelled “Updated September 27, 2026”, which does not match the tracker’s 8 October timing. The page’s hidden structured data, the code search engines read, still lists the old Secure Cloud prices, such as $3.49 for the H100 SXM [2]. The tracker says it read RunPod’s public API, and that on 9 October the page’s own markup still carried $3.49 [1]. That fits what we see.

...

- A RunPod announcement. We found none, and no reason for the rises.
- When RunPod made the change. The tracker reads hourly and gives a one-hour window.
- Other providers’ prices. This covers RunPod only.
- Every region or product. Serverless and cluster pricing are not covered.

results.title: What a million tokens costs on a rented H100 or B200 — Die Brief
highlights:
Nebius posts 4.50 dollars an hour for an H100 and 8.50 for a B200 from 8 October 2026. Lambda posts 3.99 and 6.69 on its instance page. Neither page prices a million tokens.

...

Nebius prints the rates in its document Compute pricing in Nebius AI Cloud. The page says on-demand prices for B300, B200, H200, and H100 changed on 1 October 2026, and that from 8 October 2026 the preemptible price on several of those platforms is a dynamic spot rate, displayed as a floor. The dollar figures on that page are before tax. The billing unit is one second and the pricing unit is one hour, so thirty minutes is half the hourly rate. A stopped virtual machine is not charged for the GPU. The bars are the on-demand rates read on 10 October 2026. The 8 October note on that page is a preemptible floor, and it is not drawn. The line above the bars is what an H100 hour has cost across the months a posted rate could be read.

NVIDIA B300 NVLink is 9.50 dollars for one GPU-hour, with a preemptible floor of 0.99 dollars. Before 1 October the same block lists 7.85 dollars on demand. NVIDIA B200 NVLink is 8.50 dollars for one GPU-hour. The page ties one platform id to us-central1 and another to me-west1, at the same on-demand rate, with a preemptible floor of 0.99 dollars. Before 1 October that block lists 7.15 dollars. NVIDIA H200 NVLink is 5.40 dollars, in eu-north1, eu-north2, eu-west1, and us-central1, with a preemptible floor of 0.79 dollars. Before 1 October it lists 4.50 dollars. NVIDIA H100 NVLink is 4.50 dollars, and the page says that platform is only in eu-north1. The preemptible floor is 0.79 dollars. Before 1 October it lists 3.85 dollars.

...

An H100 hour has not moved in one smooth line, and the two rates on the chart are different offers. The SXM5 pay-as-you-go hour was $4.85 from November 2023 through July 2024, and $3.50 on 15 September 2024. The later NVLink hour was $2.95 from October 2025 through May 2026, $3.85 from 1 June 2026, and $4.50 from 1 October 2026. The months between September 2024 and November 2025 are left empty. The posted offer changed, and those in-between months were not in the copies read for this brief. A third quote, $2.118 for the GPU alone with the processor and memory billed beside it, is not drawn.

The useful update is the dated move on the Nebius page itself. From 1 October 2026 the on-demand H100 line goes from 3.85 to 4.50 dollars, the H200 line from 4.50 to 5.40, the B200 line from 7.15 to 8.50, and the B300 line from 7.85 to 9.50. Those four pairs are on one document, with the old rate left in place under a "before" heading. Lambda's instance rows do not carry a date. The 6.69 and 3.99 dollar figures are what that URL showed on 10 October 2026, and a revision should open the URL again rather than treat them as a contract.

results.title: AI Compute Cost Outlook: Quarterly Briefing · AgentFlare
highlights:
### Pricing is high at the hyperscalers, discounted elsewhere

As of early November, H100 on-demand pricing ranged from roughly $6.88 per GPU-hour at AWS to $11.06 at Google Cloud, versus approximately $3.90–$6.16 across major neoclouds. [5] H200 pricing reached $10.60 per hour on Google Cloud, while B200 capacity was generally available through flexible-start or committed products rather than standard on-demand listings. [4] 

The spread is economically material: hyperscaler list prices averaged nearly twice GPU-cloud medians across H100, H200, and B200 instances. [1] This creates a strong incentive for workload migration, capacity brokering, and multicloud arbitrage—particularly for inference jobs with predictable utilization.

...

Reservation economics are increasingly decisive. One-year commitments reduce median GPU pricing by about 21%, while three-year commitments cut it by approximately 48% versus on-demand rates. [1] Google’s three-year H100 commitment was listed at $4.86 per GPU-hour, compared with an $11.06 on-demand rate; its H200 equivalent was $4.65 versus $10.60. [4] 

Spot pricing can be dramatically lower—up to 91% below on-demand in some Google configurations—but availability and interruption risk make it unsuitable as the sole basis for distributed training capacity. [4] The next quarters should therefore see more hybrid scheduling: committed capacity for critical training, spot for checkpointable jobs, and neocloud overflow for inference.

...

Expect advertised hyperscaler GPU rates to remain sticky through the next two quarters, with selective increases where supply is tight—AWS raised several U.S. GPU configurations by about 15% in October after earlier 2026 increases. [9] Effective market pricing should nevertheless decline as neocloud supply expands and long-term discounts deepen.

results.title: Why GPU prices spike during AI compute shortages | CloudPe Blog
highlights:
GPU prices spike when AI demand outpaces the memory, chip packaging, and power new GPUs need. In 2026, NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 list price rose from $8,565 to $16,000, and B200 rentals jumped 79% in three months. Yet H100 rentals fell 64% to 75% from their 2024 peak.

...

A GPU price spike is a sharp rise in what buyers pay to rent or own a GPU, usually within weeks or months. It shows up in two places: hourly cloud rates and hardware list prices. The two can move at different times and by different amounts.

Contract type matters too. Spot and on-demand rates track the market daily, while reserved contracts lock a price for a year or more. In 2026, reserved H100 prices rose about 40% while on-demand prices fell, because on-demand capacity was sold out.

## GPU prices in 2026

Cloud GPU rental prices are up 13% over 12 months across 21 models, with 16 rising and 5 falling. The GPU prices chart below shows the biggest moves. Rental figures are in US dollars per GPU-hour.

| GPU or price type | Earlier | Latest | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, one-year contract | $1.70 (Oct 2025) | $2.35 (Mar 2026) | +38% |
| H100, on-demand median | 12 months ago | $3.57 (week of 12 Oct 2026) | +19% |
| B200 rental | 3 months ago | $8.01 (Sept 2026) | +79% |
| RTX PRO 6000 list price | $8,565 (Mar 2025) | $16,000 (Aug 2026) | +87% |

Note: Trackers measure different things, so the same GPU can show different prices. On 7 October, one list-price median put the H100 at $4.20, while trade-based indexes showed about $2.81 to $2.86.

...

GPU prices spike because demand rises fast while supply cannot. New supply depends on memory, packaging, and power that take quarters or years to expand. With supply fixed, price absorbs the extra demand.

...

Prices rise first where capacity is tightest: newest GPUs, high-memory

...

| Period | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Early 2024 | H100 rentals peak at $8 to $10 an hour |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | H100 on-demand up 10% in four weeks, from $2.00 to $2.20 |
| Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contracts reach $2.35 |
| Jun 2026 | H100 eases to $2.01 to $2.53 as Blackwell supply ramps |
| 1 Oct 2026 | Nebius raises H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 |

...

Billing is in INR from a Mumbai Tier-4 data centre, with no data-transfer surcharges within India.

results.title: GPU Instance Pricing in 2026: How to Compare AWS, GCP, Azure, and Scaleway Before You Commit - Qovery Blog
highlights:
- The reliable stack has three layers: each provider's first-party calculator or pricing API as the source of truth for rates, one multi-cloud normalizer like Holori or Vantage to line them up, and a spec explorer to confirm you are comparing the same silicon.
- On-demand list prices for the same GPU swing by roughly 2x between providers and regions. A single on-demand H100 works out to about $6.88/GPU-hour on an AWS p5 node and about $12.29/GPU-hour on an Azure ND H100 v5 node (both verified October 2026), while Scaleway publishes its H100 PCIe at €2.73/GPU-hour openly in EUR with no login.
- Per-GPU-hour is the wrong unit. The number that decides anything is cost per 1,000 requests or per million tokens, and a 75% utilized expensive GPU routinely beats a 30% utilized cheap one.
- Availability is a cost line, not a footnote. Check AWS Service Quotas, GCP GPU regional availability, Azure quota per SKU, and Scaleway per-zone stock before you model anything. A cheaper region you cannot get capacity in is infinitely expensive.
- Qovery is not a GPU provider and not a pricing calculator. It is an internal developer platform that deploys your inference service into your own AWS, GCP, Azure, or Scaleway account or your existing Kubernetes cluster, so discounts stay in your name and you can re-run the same workload on a second cloud to get real cost-per-request numbers.

...

The H100 tier. A full 8x H100 node runs $55.04/hour on AWS p5.48xlarge in us-east-1 (that is $6.88 per GPU-hour, SXM with NVLink) and $98.32/hour on an Azure ND H100 v5 node in East US (about $12.29 per GPU-hour, also SXM). Scaleway sells the H100 differently, per card: €2.73/hour for a single H100 PCIe 80GB. That PCIe-vs-SXM difference matters for multi-GPU training, which is exactly why you confirm the interconnect before you compare. Google's A3 (8x H100) price is published on the GCP GPU pricing page, but that table renders through a client-side calculator, so I am not going to quote a number I could not read straight from Google. Pull it live in the console or via the Billing Catalog API.

The inference-realistic tier. For single-GPU serving: AWS g6e.xlarge (1x L40S 48GB) is $1.861/hour and g6.xlarge (1x L4) is $0.8048/hour in us-east-1. On Scaleway, an L40S is €1.47/hour and an L4 is €0.79/hour. Azure's smaller GPU lineup is shaped differently: the closest single-card option is the NC40ads H100 v5 (1x H100 NVL) at $6.98/hour in East US, since Azure does not offer an L4-class VM. GCP's G2 (L4) price lives on the same JS-rendered pricing page, so verify it live.

| Provider | Instance | GPU (count) | VRAM/GPU | Region | On-demand/hr | $/GPU-hr | Commitment | Spot? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | p5.48xlarge | H100 SXM (8) | 80 GB | us-east-1 | $55.04 | ~$6.88 | 1yr/3yr | Yes |
| Azure | ND H100 v5 | H100 SXM (8) | 80 GB | East US | $98.32 | ~$12.29 | 1yr/3yr | Yes |
| GCP | A3 highgpu-8g | H100 SXM (8) | 80 GB | US | verify live (JS calc) | verify live | 1yr/3yr | Yes |
| Scaleway | H100-1-80G | H100 PCIe (1) | 80 GB | PAR-2 | €2.73 | €2.73 | - | - |
| AWS | g6e.xlarge | L40S (1) | 48 GB | us-east-1 | $1.861 | $1.861 | 1yr/3yr | Yes |
| AWS | g6.xlarge | L4 (1) | 24 GB | us-east-1 | $0.8048 | $0.8048 | 1yr/3yr | Yes |
| Scaleway | L40S-1-48G | L40S (1) | 48 GB | PAR-2 | €1.47 | €1.47 | - | - |
| Scaleway | L4-1-24G | L4 (1) | 24 GB | PAR-2 | €0.79 | €0.79 | - | - |
| Azure | NC40ads H100 v5 | H100 NVL (1) | 94 GB | East US | $6.98 | $6.98 | 1yr/3yr | Yes |
| GCP | G2 standard | L4 (1) | 24 GB | US | verify live (JS calc) | verify live | 1yr/3yr | Yes |

...

None of the three publishes a clean fixed 1-year-vs-3-year percentage per GPU SKU, so treat the headline numbers as ceilings and price your actual term in the calculator. For batch and offline work, spot is strong: AWS advertises up to 90%, GCP up to 91%, and Azure quotes no fixed number but its live spot rates for the ND H100 v5 run roughly 80% below on-demand in some regions. Spot is fine for offline inference and dangerous for anything with a latency SLA.

...

Because the only number that decides anything is cost per unit served - cost per 1,000 requests or per million tokens - and utilization moves that number more than the hourly rate does. A cheaper GPU you run at 30% utilization will quietly lose to a pricier one you run at 75%.

Here is the formula, written out:

◆ Pull quote

cost per 1,000 requests = ($/GPU-hour ÷ requests served per hour) x 1,000

A worked example with illustrative numbers (these are made up to show the math, not sourced prices):

- Option A: a cheaper card at $2.00/GPU-hour that, with your model and traffic shape, effectively serves 4,000 requests/hour. Cost per 1,000 = (2.00 ÷ 4,000) x 1,000 = $0.50.
- Option B: a pricier card at $3.50/GPU-hour that serves 12,000 requests/hour because the model fits better and batches more efficiently. Cost per 1,000 = (3.50 ÷ 12,000) x 1,000 = $0.29.

...

That inversion is the whole point.

results.title: 323 Nvidia GPU Rental Providers and B200 Spot Prices Up 2x: Inside the Neocloud Boom Updated November 15 - AIReport.NET
highlights:
SemiAnalysis counts 323 providers renting Nvidia GPUs as of September, up 55% in under 11 months, and B200 spot prices have more than doubled since March. CNBC maps the tiers from hyperscalers to baby neoclouds, with SpaceX charging Anthropic $1.25 billion a month and five customers now each representing at least 10% of Nvidia receivables.

...

Hence the neoclouds. Modal, a startup running sandboxes for AI agents, now buys from 25 of them, says CEO Erik Bernhardsson. CoreWeave's near-term capacity is essentially sold out, per CEO Michael Intrator, and even Google and Microsoft have started renting from CoreWeave while competing with it. Below the brands, specialist providers like Runpod and Massed Compute sell flexibility — hourly bare-metal GPUs — into a market where the hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 has more than doubled since March, according to the index maintained by Ornn.

results.title: WSJ: AI Compute Power Shortage Deepens — H100 Rental… — Aishunos
highlights:
Context: artificial intelligence companies face a shortage of graphics processors (GPUs) needed to train models and serve them. On October 10, 2026, The Wall Street Journal, citing SemiAnalysis data, reported that the hourly rental rate for Nvidia H100 under one-year contracts rose 60% in a year. What changed: demand for AI compute reached unprecedented levels, on-demand capacity is fully sold out across all GPU types, and leading AI labs — from Anthropic to Meta — are seeking capacity even from rivals. 📎 Sources: The Wall Street Journal (https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/ai-computing-power-demand-a63da9b9), SemiAnalysis (https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/the-great-gpu-shortage-rental-capacity)

...

The Wall Street Journal reported on October 10, 2026, that demand for artificial intelligence compute power is growing at an unprecedented rate. The publication described the situation as a "desperate hunt" for AI compute: companies are struggling to find the graphics processors needed to train models and serve them. Citing data from research firm SemiAnalysis, the WSJ wrote that the rental price of Nvidia's H100 graphics processor under one-year contracts rose 60% over the past year. Meanwhile, Alphabet plans up to $200 billion in capital expenditure this year — much of it directed at AI infrastructure.

...

According to SemiAnalysis's analysis, the company's H100 one-year rental price index is compiled from a monthly survey of more than 100 market participants and confirmed with deal data. The index shows the price per GPU-hour rose from $1.70 in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026 — a gain of nearly 40%. The increase was especially rapid: the index's lowest point came in October 2025 itself, and contract prices surged over the following six months.

On-demand GPU capacity, meanwhile, is fully sold out across all GPU types. That means almost no spare capacity remains on the market — companies needing new capacity must wait in line or pay high prices on the contract market. According to the WSJ, some companies are trying to expand capacity under existing contracts, but supply is lagging behind demand.

results.title: Rent GPU for AI 2026: hourly prices compared
highlights:
In short

- Rent by the hour unless the card runs almost around the clock: divide the monthly price by the hourly one and you get the number of hours after which the monthly plan wins. For an A100 at Cherry Servers that is about 702 of 730 hours in a month.
- Choose by VRAM, not by model name: 24 GB covers SDXL, Flux and 7B LLMs, 48 GB is the comfortable middle, and 80 GB (A100, H100) is for fine-tuning and 70B models in 4-bit.
- Prices from the official pages, October 2026: RunPod has the RTX 4090 at $0.89/h, A100 80 GB at $1.79/h and H100 SXM at $3.99/h; DigitalOcean has L40S at $1.57/h and H100 at $4.41/h; Cherry Servers lists the A100 from $2.362/h.
- Look past the hourly rate: a stopped volume disk on RunPod costs $0.20/GB a month, DigitalOcean keeps billing a powered-off Droplet, and RunPod terminates pods without a network volume when your balance reaches zero.

...

## Hourly cloud or a dedicated GPU server

With hourly cloud you start a machine, pay per second or per hour, and delete it when the job ends. A dedicated GPU server is a whole physical machine rented for a month or longer, and at some providers by the hour too. For most jobs the first is cheaper, and the arithmetic fits on one line: divide the monthly price by the hourly price and you get the number of hours after which the monthly plan starts to win.

Cherry Servers lists an A100 80 GB from $2.362/h and from $1,657.68/month. Divide: about 702 hours, or 96% of a 730-hour month. The monthly discount is nearly invisible unless the card runs without a break. RunPod asks $1.79/h for an A100, which is about $1,307 for 730 hours. On these listed rates the cloud is cheaper even if you never switch it off.

...

| GPU (VRAM) | RunPod, $/h | Fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 3090 (24 GB) | 0.50 | SDXL and Flux, 7B LLMs (≈14 GB), quantised models up to 13B |
| RTX 4090 (24 GB) | 0.89 | the same jobs, faster |
| L40S (48 GB) | 1.09 | larger quantised LLMs, big image batches, LoRA training |
| A100 (80 GB) | 1.79 | fine-tuning 7B–13B, 70B in 4-bit (≈35 GB) |
| H100 SXM (80 GB) | 3.99 | training, high-throughput inference |
| H200 (141 GB) | 5.29 | 70B at 16-bit is a squeeze: weights alone are ≈140 GB, little room for long context |

Source: runpod.io/pricing, Pods list, per the provider's site, October 2026.

...

## What an hour costs: providers compared

| Provider | Cards and prices | Billing | Traffic | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | RTX 4090 24 GB — $0.89/h; A100 80 GB — $1.79/h; H100 SXM — $3.99/h | per second; about an hour of credit needed to deploy | no ingress or egress fees | experiments, fine-tuning, SD and Flux, Serverless inference |
| DigitalOcean | RTX 4000 Ada 20 GB — $0.76/h; L40S 48 GB — $1.57/h; H100 80 GB — $4.41/h; MI300X 192 GB — $2.59/h | per second, 5-minute minimum; a stopped Droplet is still billed | 10,000–15,000 GiB included, overage price not stated | teams whose app already runs on DigitalOcean |
| Cherry Servers | A2 16 GB — from $0.239/h; A40 48 GB — from $0.801/h; A100 80 GB — from $2.362/h | hourly, monthly, yearly | 30–100 TB of free egress | a dedicated GPU server; the page lists Lithuania, some models are pre-order or waiting list |
| Vultr | a Cloud GPU line exists, the price page did not open, so no figures | — | — | compare on the live page; $300 credit for new users for 30 days |

Source: RunPod, DigitalOcean and Cherry Servers price pages, per the provider's site, October 2026.

Two observations. RunPod is cheaper on cards of the same class: the L40S is $1.09/h there against $1.57 at DigitalOcean, and the H100 is $3.99 against $4.41. But it is a GPU-only platform, so your database and web app have to live somewhere else. DigitalOcean costs more per hour, yet a GPU Droplet sits in the same account, network and API as the rest of your infrastructure. Cherry Servers is the only one of the three that hands you a whole physical machine with a big traffic allowance. Its A40 and A100 are marked as pre-order, so check stock before you pay.

...

The other source of discounts is spot, meaning machines that can be taken back. DigitalOcean lists spot GPU Droplets only for the newest data-centre cards (for example the B300 at $6.17/h). It aims to give at least two hours' notice but may reclaim a machine with less or none, and it locks the price at creation. Spot suits jobs that save checkpoints and resume. It is a poor fit for a demo in front of a customer.

...

## Hidden costs: disks, traffic and idle time

- Disk. At RunPod a container disk costs $0.10/GB a month and is erased when the pod stops. A volume disk costs $0.10/GB a month while running and $0.20/GB while stopped. A network volume is $0.07/GB a month under 1 TB and does not depend on a pod. For 200 GB of models that is $20 running, $40 stopped, or $14 on a network volume.
- Traffic. RunPod's docs state no fees for data ingress or egress. DigitalOcean includes 10,000–15,000 GiB in a GPU Droplet plan but gives no overage price. Cherry Servers lists 30–100 TB of free egress.
- Idle time. DigitalOcean keeps billing a powered-off Droplet because the disk, CPU, RAM and IP stay reserved; only destroying it stops the meter. An RTX 4090 at $0.89/h forgotten over a weekend (48 hours) costs about $43.
- Balance. At RunPod you need roughly an hour of credit to deploy. When the balance reaches $0, pods stop, and those without a network volume are terminated with their data, which cannot be recovered.
